preamble.text: Historical snapshot: later evidence may be reflected in current research pages and corrections.
Deterministically compiled from canonical evidence. Importance measures impact, not truth; evidence/confidence remain separate.

blocks.text: 1. Tencent Hy4 preview combines 770B MoE capacity with sparse attention, IndexCache and native MTP

Desk: architectures_scaling Evidence: A · confirmed · active · importance 8/10 (Field-shifting) What changed: Tencent released Hy4 preview under Apache-2.0 with a 770B-parameter MoE backbone, 49B active parameters per token, 1M context, Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention, cross-layer IndexCache reuse, four-stream identity Hyper-Connections, and a native MTP layer intended for speculative decoding. Tencent lists API prices of CNY 6 per million input tokens, CNY 18 per million output tokens and cache-hit prices from CNY 0.3; its separate 31.8% throughput gain is a vendor claim without enough matched measurement detail for independent comparison. Why it matters: Hy4 is a third major open-weight frontier release in the same week emphasizing sparse long-context retrieval and richer residual routing, while also shipping native multi-token prediction. It strengthens the architectural-convergence signal but does not by itself establish that these mechanisms outperform matched dense or hybrid alternatives. The official Chinese release also supplies concrete API prices and a vendor-reported 31.8% throughput gain, while leaving total cost, matched serving conditions and independent confirmation open.

Demonstrated: Released BF16/FP8 model artifacts and configuration expose a 770B backbone with 49B active parameters per token, 1M context, 256 routed experts, top-8 routing, Gated DSA, four residual streams and native MTP. Apache-2.0 licensing is present in the released artifact.

Claimed: Tencent reports its largest generation-over-generation capability gain and small wins over GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 in an internal blind evaluation of 163 experts across 203 engineering tasks. Tencent’s Chinese release additionally reports an internal blind evaluation of 163 experts over 203 engineering tasks (mean 2.99/4 vs. GLM 5.3 at 2.92/4 and Kimi K3 at 2.94/4), and a 31.8% end-to-end throughput gain over an unspecified baseline after model-led operator optimization; both remain vendor claims.

Mechanism: A 78-layer MoE backbone: one dense FFN layer followed by 77 MoE layers with 256 routed experts plus one shared expert; top-8 routed experts are active per token. Attention uses Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention with IndexCache to reuse sparse indices across layers. The residual path uses four-stream identity Hyper-Connections. A separate native MTP layer adds 10B total/0.7B active parameters for speculative decoding.
Strongest baseline: Tencent's internal blind comparison against GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3; no matched-compute architectural ablation is supplied in the release card.

Regime: Frontier-scale 770B-total/49B-active open-weight model; serving remains hardware-heavy despite sparse activation. Internal productivity evaluation is vendor-run and not an independent reproduction.

Limitations: The strongest quality comparison disclosed in the model card is vendor-run and narrowly separated from GLM-5.3/Kimi K3; it is not independent evidence.; No matched-compute ablation isolates the contribution of sparse attention, IndexCache, iHC or native MTP.; 49B active parameters still implies a heavy local serving regime; sparse activation does not make the 770B stored model a small local model.; Tencent explicitly notes overlong reasoning and over-verification in this preview.; Tencent’s Chinese release reports a 31.8% end-to-end throughput improvement after model-led operator optimization, but the inspected statement does not give enough hardware, request-load or baseline detail to reproduce or generalize it.; Published API token prices do not establish total cost of ownership, local deployment cost, or throughput-adjusted unit economics.

Open evidence gaps: No matched training/inference budget ablation establishes the isolated gains from Gated DSA, IndexCache, iHC or native MTP.; Vendor quality and productivity results lack independent reproduction.

Sources: https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy4-preview · https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy4-preview/blob/main/config.json · https://www.tencent.com/tencent-releases-and-open-sources-tencent-hy4-preview/ · https://www.tencent.com/zh-cn/tencent-releases-and-open-sources-tencent-hy4-preview/
2. Anthropic reports Claude leads 26% of measured AI R&D while none is fully autonomous

Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · strongly_supported · active · importance 8/10 (Field-shifting) Importance rationale: If sustained and independently validated, AI leading a quarter of frontier-lab R&D while collaborating on over 90% materially changes the speed and structure of frontier development and creates a measurable precursor to stronger recursive acceleration; it is field-shifting but not evidence of autonomous RSI.

What changed: Anthropic published a prototype R&D Automation Index based on roughly 15,000 sampled granular R&D tasks organized into 378 leaf categories and rated on Epoch AI's AL0-AL5 automation scale. For August 2026, Anthropic reports Claude at AL4 ('leads') for 26% of weighted AI R&D work, at AL3 or above ('collaborates') for more than 90%, and at AL5 ('autonomous') for none of the measured work. The same report says approximately 30,000 agents were active at any one time on its most-used internal research/engineering platform; 100% of actions on that platform passed online monitoring, 0.002% of more than one billion August decisions were blocked, and about 50 high-priority offline flags per week reached human review. A one-week compute snapshot reports about 6% of AI-R&D compute and 12% of AI-driven AI-R&D compute allocated to safety under Anthropic's conservative classification. Why it matters: This is unusually concrete first-party evidence about the production process of frontier-model R&D rather than a benchmark proxy. If the methodology survives independent audit and becomes comparable across labs, it gives the field a measurable way to track AI-driven acceleration, oversight load and safety-compute allocation before fully autonomous recursive self-improvement. The reported 26% AL4 share is material, but the explicit zero-AL5 result is equally important: it argues for rapid partial automation, not autonomous self-improvement today.

Demonstrated: Within Anthropic's internal measurement system, August 2026 ratings put 26% of weighted AI R&D at AL4, over 90% at AL3+, and 0% at AL5. Model-vs-human exact automation-rating agreement is reported as 59%, human-vs-human as 35%, with model and human within one level 97% of the time. On the measured agent platform, online monitor coverage is reported at 100%, with 0.002% of over one billion August decisions blocked.

Claimed: Anthropic argues these metrics can give the public and governments visibility into the pace of frontier development and could support cross-lab reporting, independent verification and pacing triggers.

Mechanism: A frozen taxonomy of 378 leaf R&D task categories is built from sampled internal work records. Claude research agents gather evidence on how each category is performed, an independent Claude judge assigns Epoch AI AL0-AL5 automation levels, and categories are weighted by sampled person-time. Separate platform telemetry measures agent-monitor coverage, review latency and block/escalation rates; compute accounting classifies R&D workloads by purpose.
Strongest baseline: The most relevant baseline is Anthropic's own February 2026 AL4 share, reported as under 1%; cross-lab comparison is not yet valid because methodology is not standardized.
Regime: Anthropic internal AI R&D and its most-used internal research/engineering agent platform; August 2026 automation/oversight snapshot plus July 13-20 compute snapshot.

Limitations: Automation ratings and much of the evidence extraction use Claude itself, creating correlated-judge risk.; Underlying internal work records and telemetry are unavailable for independent audit.; Person-time weighting is a crude proxy for contribution to model progress and may underweight rare bottleneck tasks.; The 30,000-agent oversight figures cover only Anthropic's most-used internal platform, not all company agent activity.; Cross-lab comparisons are currently invalid without common task definitions, weighting and independent verification.; A high AL4 share does not imply equivalent acceleration in end-to-end model capability because compute and non-automatable bottlenecks can dominate.

Open evidence gaps: No independent third party has yet verified the reported automation levels, weighting or monitor telemetry.; The 378-leaf task tree, per-category ratings, weights and raw sampled evidence are not publicly available.
Sources: https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development
3. OpenAI manuscript claims the irrationality exponent of π is exactly 2

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 8/10 (Field-shifting) Importance rationale: If true, μ(π)=2 would settle a longstanding number-theory problem and substantially strengthen Diophantine approximation for π, with implications for related analytic questions. The claim is field-shifting in consequence; its truth remains unverified and must be evaluated separately.

What changed: OpenAI’s 23-page manuscript claims that for every ν>2 there is a threshold Q(ν) such that |π−p/q|≥q^-ν for all integers p and q≥Q(ν), and concludes that π has irrationality exponent 2. If correct, this would sharply improve the prior upper bounds discussed in the paper. The threshold is ineffective; the manuscript does not prove a uniform c/q² lower bound or bounded continued-fraction partial quotients. OpenAI’s public family-017 note describes a Lean statement covering the exponent claim, but no independent build, semantic audit or number-theory review was performed here. Treat the theorem as claimed, not established. Why it matters: An independently verified exponent of 2 for π would settle a long-standing Diophantine-approximation question and affect related number-theory results. The implication is unusually large, while the current evidence remains an unreviewed first-party paper and formalization claim.
Claimed: The manuscript claims μ(π)=2, equivalently that for every ν>2 there is Q(ν) such that all integer p and q≥Q(ν) satisfy |π−p/q|≥q^-ν.

Mechanism: The manuscript presents an interpolation/determinant argument to derive an eventual lower bound |π−p/q|≥q^-ν for each fixed ν>2. Its formalization note identifies a selected Lean theorem for the irrationality-exponent statement.

Strongest baseline: The paper cites prior upper bounds 7.103205334137… (Zeilberger–Zudilin, 2020) and <7.101862832357 (Bai, 2026). The new claim, if valid, is a large improvement; these baselines are themselves published mathematical results and are not independently audited here.
Regime: Classical irrationality exponent of π, with a non-effective threshold depending on each ν>2. The result does not imply a uniform constant c/q² or bounded partial quotients.

Sources: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a/preprints/The-irrationality-exponent-of-pi-is-2-September-24-2026/paper.pdf · https://github.com/openai/math/blob/adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a/lean/docs/017.md · https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11276 · https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.06345 · https://github.com/openai/math/blob/adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a/lean/OAI/NumberTheory/PiExponent/Main.lean · https://github.com/openai/math/blob/adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a/lean/ComparatorChallenges/PiExponent.lean · https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mathvet/mathvet/main/reviews/openai-math/challenge-status.csv · https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-irrationality-exponent-of-pi-is-2-September-24-2026/build/main.tex
4. A collaborative AI laboratory reports a theory-led diamond-spin experiment

Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 7/10 (Very major) Importance rationale: If reproduced and extended, agents that reject an inadequate experimental design, preserve inconclusive outcomes when controls fail, and revise an acquisition without relaxing criteria could materially change AI-assisted experimental research. This single paper reports one bounded diamond-spin calibration study and does not establish general autonomous science capability.

What changed: A preprint reports a collaborative LLM-agent laboratory that derived and tested a calibration law for ensembles of nitrogen-vacancy spins in diamond. The agents rejected an initial design because ordinary interpolation could make the same predictions, then classified an acquisition as inconclusive when phase and reference controls failed during signal drift. Authors report that agents revised the protocol without relaxing precommitted criteria; a six-hour randomized acquisition then passed the stated controls and supported predictions on four withheld pulse sequences. These are author-reported results from one laboratory study. The public Auctopus repository’s README says its mock-model offline demo does not reproduce the paper and that study prompts are not included; experimental data and analysis are available from the corresponding author on request. Why it matters: This paper reports a concrete example of agents altering a physical-science study after identifying a nondiscriminating design and failed controls, while retaining the original acceptance criteria. If independently reproduced beyond this single diamond-spin task, that workflow could improve the reliability of AI-directed experiments. The paper does not demonstrate broad autonomous research capability or establish independent validation of its own claims.
Demonstrated: The arXiv v1 HTML paper, methods, acquisition protocol, abstract and data/code statements were inspected. No underlying data were obtained and no independent reproduction was conducted.

Claimed: Authors report a collaborative agent workflow that derived a calibration law for a defined nitrogen-vacancy spin setting, rejected a design that could not distinguish the law from interpolation, classified a control-failed run as inconclusive, then supported predictions with a revised six-hour acquisition under retained criteria.

Mechanism: Specialized agents propose, critique and gate the research question, theoretical derivation, computational checks, experimental design and analysis. The paper reports independent controls and precommitted acceptance rules; failed controls led to an inconclusive classification and revised acquisition.

Strongest baseline: The paper states the initial design was insufficient because Fourier interpolation could predict its withheld targets. In the revised design, the reported calibration law and two specified interpolation methods made distinct predictions for four withheld targets; authors report the final measurements supported the law within precommitted criteria.

Regime: One laboratory study of nitrogen-vacancy spin ensembles in diamond using microwave-pulse calibration; four withheld targets in the final experimental comparison. The paper reports a six-hour final acquisition with 21,600 one-second records.

Limitations: All claims about the experiment and agent decisions are author-reported; no independent reproduction was conducted here.; The study is limited to one laboratory and one nitrogen-vacancy spin calibration task.; The linked Auctopus repository does not reproduce the study from its offline demo: it uses mock models and local folders, and the paper prompts are not included.; The preprint states that data and analysis are available on reasonable request; independent access was not confirmed in this review.

Open evidence gaps: Underlying measurement data and analysis were not independently available during this review; authors say they are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.; The report describes one diamond NV-spin calibration task; transfer to other apparatus, experimental domains and autonomous workflows is not established.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40589 · https://github.com/E-zClap/auctopus
5. OpenAI describes expanded frontier-model misalignment monitoring and a live training alert

Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 7/10 (Very major) Importance rationale: If the reported monitoring system detects consequential agent behavior across frontier training, evaluation, internal use and selected external deployments, it could materially change how frontier systems are contained and safety cases are evaluated. Coverage and effectiveness remain first-party claims.

What changed: OpenAI’s Oct 29 disclosure describes a layered system for monitoring frontier-model training, evaluations, internal agent use and selected external tool use. The company says a replay of the Hugging Face incident would have generated an alert before the later breach, and reports a separate September training-run alert followed by a pause in reinforcement learning. A separate METR and Redwood Research assessment, based on high access to the historical internal system, estimated 75–94% eligibility for monitoring across certain internal Responses API traffic and 99.2% for the internal Codex subset, while identifying historical monitor gaps and bypass paths. Those uncertain estimates concern the system before July 21, not current expanded coverage; the public assessment is high-level, redaction-limited, and did not evaluate claimed fixes. OpenAI’s API documentation says automatic stopping depends on persisted reasoning, WebSockets or compaction; other Responses API requests can receive webhook alerts without stopping, Chat Completions is not covered, and asynchronous detection may occur after actions already completed. Why it matters: Monitoring is presented as a detection and response layer alongside alignment training and access controls. METR and Redwood’s high-access assessment found historical gaps and bypass paths, while OpenAI reports subsequent expansion and alerts. OpenAI’s API documentation makes the operational boundary concrete: automatic stopping requires supported conversation continuity, detection is asynchronous, and some API paths are alert-only or excluded. The independent assessment does not measure the current system; current effectiveness remains unresolved.

Demonstrated: The public sources document OpenAI’s stated current architecture and incident timings, plus METR and Redwood’s account of a high-access assessment of the historical monitor. OpenAI’s API docs further define request-level scope: eligible Responses requests with persisted reasoning, WebSockets or compaction can be stopped; other Responses requests can be monitored with webhook alerts only; Chat Completions is excluded. The assessors did not evaluate the expanded system or claimed fixes, so current system effectiveness is not independently established.

Claimed: OpenAI reports a layered monitoring system spanning selected frontier training, evaluation, internal use and external tool-use surfaces. METR and Redwood report historical eligibility estimates and monitor vulnerabilities from a high-access review of the earlier internal system.

Mechanism: OpenAI describes a low-cost activation-probe layer routing cases to model-based review, then investigative agents and, for sensitive workloads, checks against network logs and other telemetry. Its API guide says external monitoring is asynchronous and can trigger a safety.alert.created event; automatic stopping requires supported conversation continuity via persisted reasoning, WebSockets or compaction. Without those mechanisms the request can continue despite an alert, and Chat Completions is outside this monitor. METR and Redwood report historical bypass paths in the earlier internal system; OpenAI says the newer system has expanded, but assessors did not evaluate it.

Strongest baseline: METR and Redwood report historical eligibility estimates of 75–94% for certain internal Responses API traffic and 99.2% for the Codex subset, while identifying uncovered traffic and monitor-bypass paths. These are uncertain eligibility estimates, not end-to-end effectiveness measures; the assessment predates the expanded system and supplies no current matched baseline. Current API docs specify a stop-eligible subset and excluded Chat Completions requests but provide no independent measured detection or response rates.

Regime: OpenAI’s Oct 29 description of monitoring for frontier-model reinforcement learning, evaluations, internal Codex traffic and selected external tool use; the API documentation’s current request-level coverage distinctions; plus METR and Redwood’s high-access assessment of the internal monitor as it existed on and before July 21, 2026. The historical estimates and vulnerabilities are not measurements of current expanded coverage.

Limitations: OpenAI’s system, incident and timing statements are first-party reports. METR and Redwood provide an external high-access assessment of the earlier internal monitor, but their public post summarizes a 61-page internal report and OpenAI retained discretionary redaction rights.; The METR/Redwood exercise assessed the system as it existed on and before July 21, 2026, and explicitly did not evaluate the expanded system’s current coverage.; The historical 75–94%, 99.2% and roughly 10% figures are uncertain estimates about eligibility or missed traffic in specified internal workloads and periods; they are not current coverage or end-to-end detection rates.; The replayed Hugging Face alert is a simulation, not an alert observed during the original event. The reported September live alert remains an OpenAI account.; OpenAI says it patched production-stack vulnerabilities found by the assessors, but the assessors state they did not evaluate those claims.; OpenAI says external monitoring does not routinely escalate cases to its staff; API auto-pausing depends on supported conversation tracking, and Chat Completions requests are not covered.; OpenAI documentation specifies that asynchronous monitoring may alert after a consequential tool action has already completed; stopping a request does not undo earlier actions.; According to OpenAI’s API docs, automatic stopping is available only for monitored Responses API requests using persisted reasoning, WebSockets or compaction; requests without these mechanisms can receive webhooks but may continue, and Chat Completions API requests are excluded from this monitor.; No API request, webhook delivery, or automatic-stop path was exercised in this research run.

Open evidence gaps: No independent evaluation of the expanded current monitor’s end-to-end performance, alert quality or response effectiveness was inspected. METR and Redwood assessed the earlier system and explicitly did not evaluate the expanded coverage or claimed patches.; Current denominators and false-positive/false-negative rates by workload, model, surface and monitor layer are unavailable in the inspected public sources. Historical eligibility estimates do not establish current coverage.; OpenAI documentation now specifies that Responses API auto-stopping requires persisted reasoning, WebSockets or compaction; requests without these are monitored with webhook alerts but cannot be automatically stopped; Chat Completions is excluded. The checks are asynchronous and may occur after an action completed. No live API exercise or independent operation check was performed.

Sources: https://openai.com/index/how-we-detect-frontier-model-misalignment/ · https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/ · https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-checks/misalignment-monitoring · https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001509-why-was-my-chat-paused-or-ended-as-a-precaution
6. Japan begins phased government AI-agent rollout under a new governance standard

Desk: policy_geopolitics Evidence: A · confirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If implemented across Japan’s ministries, agent access for an eligible workforce of about 180,000 plus a shared governance and security standard could materially shape public-sector AI deployment and provide a model other governments assess. The announcement is a phased plan; broad usage and measurable public-service effects are not yet established.

What changed: Japan’s Digital Agency announced a staged expansion of Government AI Gennai to agent workflows and published a governance, security and safety standard. On October 30, it said a prototype app for parliamentary-answer drafting would be offered to about 180,000 government employees for trial use; 102 staff from 16 ministries had helped evaluate its development. A Japanese implementation deck reports that about 80% of evaluator-survey respondents wanted to use the prototype, but does not give the number of respondents or survey method. Human review and final responsibility remain with staff. The announcements and survey statement establish program scope and reported intent, not actual adoption or measured productivity, accuracy or safety outcomes. Why it matters: Japan’s government is moving from a broad agent-platform plan toward a concrete, high-stakes drafting use case, with an announced trial and staff evaluators across 16 ministries. The program’s governance rules and required human checks are relevant to public-sector deployment. Neither access at scale nor improvements in answer quality, time, cost or safety have been measured in the cited releases.

Demonstrated: The Japanese-language agency releases, standard and implementation deck publicly describe the Gennai rollout plan, stated rules and October 30 prototype trial announcement. They do not verify employee access or use, nor provide measured deployment outcomes; no independent audit was conducted in this activation.

Claimed: The Digital Agency announced a phased Government AI rollout to an eligible workforce of about 180,000 and says a prototype parliamentary-answer drafting app would be offered from October 30 for trial use during the 222nd extraordinary Diet session. The agency reports that about 80% of evaluator-survey respondents wanted to use the prototype; the respondent count and survey method are unspecified, so this is stated intent rather than adoption or efficacy evidence. Its standards require human oversight and source checking; no measured performance results are reported.

Mechanism: Agent Chat lets employees instruct agents to perform multi-step tasks and generate files; Gennai Workshop is intended as a personal environment for building web applications and agents; Gennai Library is intended for cross-government sharing of reusable skills. Central administration, role-based duties, data controls, human oversight and logs form the governance model.

Strongest baseline: The agency describes the prior Gennai service as chat and prepared AI applications for general tasks; it says these are insufficient for some multi-step work involving several files, large datasets, web research or administrative decision criteria. This is the agency’s rationale, not an independent comparative evaluation.

Regime: Japan Digital Agency Government AI Gennai program; intended phased ministry rollout to about 180,000 eligible staff. Agent Chat rollout started in October 2026; a parliamentary-answer support app prototype was announced for trial during the 222nd extraordinary Diet session, with full offering planned from January 2027; Gennai Workshop remains targeted for December 2026. These are program announcements, not measured deployment results.

Limitations: The roughly 180,000 figure is the eligible workforce scope, not a count of users with access or actual users.; The agency describes a world-first initiative, but this priority claim was not independently assessed and is not needed for the bounded account.; Planned target dates for Gennai Workshop and Gennai OSS Ver. 2.0 are not completed delivery.; The standard documents stated rules and design requirements; this activation did not verify operational compliance or model-provider contracts.; The October 30 parliamentary-answer app release announces prototype availability and a trial; it does not establish how many employees accessed or used it or any effect on answer quality, time, errors or cost.; The Japanese implementation deck reports about 80% evaluator-survey intent to use, but gives no respondent denominator or survey method; stated intent does not establish subsequent usage or task effects.

Open evidence gaps: The announcement sets rollout targets but does not report ministry-by-ministry availability, active-user counts or agent invocation frequency.; No measured productivity, service quality, error, safety-incident, user-satisfaction or cost results are reported for the agent rollout.; The Gennai Standard describes governance and data-handling requirements, but this review did not audit system implementation, vendor contracts, model choices, logging configuration or adherence in operation.; The October 30 parliamentary-answer app announcement sets out a trial and planned January 2027 full offering but reports no actual access or use, answer-quality, accuracy, time-saving, error or cost results.

Sources: https://www.digital.go.jp/policies/genai/agent-safety-standard · https://www.digital.go.jp/assets/contents/node/basic_page/field_ref_resources/b033337d-dad1-4493-9316-d929597e4667/9bbaf559/20261020_policies_genai_guideline_02.pdf · https://www.digital.go.jp/assets/contents/node/basic_page/field_ref_resources/b033337d-dad1-4493-9316-d929597e4667/aaad4788/20261020_policies_genai_guideline_03.pdf · https://www.digital.go.jp/policies/genai/b736d2d7-b03b-43f0-9932-eba7da7f8142
7. Rewindable proofs give weak verifiers a new route to check robust computations

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If independently checked and made practical, a sound proof protocol that lets a weak verifier check robust computations by rewinding an untrusted model could improve scalable oversight without assuming a truthful model or cryptographic commitments. The result is a theoretical construction with narrow proof-of-concept experiments; deployment relevance is not established.

What changed: A new paper introduces rewindable interactive proofs, in which a verifier can restore an AI prover to a saved interaction state and ask new questions from there. For robust oracle computations, the authors prove a relativizing protocol with a succinct verifier and a linear-time honest prover, without assuming that a prover is truthful or using cryptography. The paper reports a proof-of-concept MNIST experiment and a BLAKE3 comparison, while explicitly saying the experiments are not a realistic scalable-oversight benchmark. A linked public repository supplies code, result ledgers and scripts, but clarifies that timed runs do not restore a machine state; general preprocessing and real model-state restoration costs remain unresolved, so deployed oversight benefits are not established. Why it matters: If independently checked and made practical, rewinding a model controlled by the verifier could give scalable oversight a new way to check some robust computations without trusting a prover or using cryptographic commitments. The paper-linked repository makes the implementation and shipped results inspectable, but its timing experiments do not execute machine-state restoration. The formal result is restricted to robust oracle computations, and preprocessing, realistic tasks and full state-restore costs remain unresolved.

Demonstrated: The paper-linked public repository contains Rust implementation code, shipped result ledgers, reproduction scripts and selected MNIST bundles. Its README says the reported timing runs execute the honest prover and time its messages and answers; they do not restore a machine state. These are inspectable author-provided artifacts, not an independent reproduction. The largest MNIST rerun is resource-intensive, with the README specifying about 400 GB memory and a 1 TiB machine.

Claimed: The authors' informal Theorem 1.1 constructs a relativizing RIP for ε-robust oracle circuits. After preprocessing, the verifier runs in Õ(n+m+1/ε) time and makes O(1/ε) oracle queries; the honest prover runs in O(n+m+S)+Õ(1/ε), with soundness error at most 1/3 against an unbounded cheating prover. Experiments report 74–80 verifier queries on selected MNIST-derived circuits up to 2^26 views and 1.8–2.1× BLAKE3 prover speedups over Flock's SNARG in medians of three runs.

Mechanism: The verifier saves the prover model’s interaction state when a proof string is fixed, then restores that state to query portions of the string. Because the prover cannot condition a saved answer on later verifier messages, rewindability substitutes for cryptographic commitments in the authors’ formal protocol. The measurements implement the protocol’s query/answer logic but, as the linked repository clarifies, they do not perform a physical machine-state restore. The proof covers computations whose outputs tolerate changes to a small fraction of oracle answers.

Strongest baseline: For BLAKE3, the authors compare their RIP compilation to Flock’s SNARG prover and report 1.8–2.1× lower prover time, medians of three executions on one Graviton 4 core. The comparison changes interactive security parameters and field configuration. The repository says the timed runs measure honest-prover messages and answers without restoring machine state. For the selected MNIST circuits, direct table lookup is the baseline; the verifier is faster only at the largest sizes, while the prover remains about 60× slower than direct evaluation.

Regime: Formal relativizing interactive proof for robust oracle-aided Boolean circuits, plus a Rust implementation evaluated on selected MNIST-derived majority circuits and an adapted BLAKE3 proof workload. The theorem assumes prover-state rewindability; the experiments do not include realistic model inference or state-copy cost.

Limitations: This is a single v1 preprint; the formal proof and reported measurements were not independently reviewed or reproduced in this activation.; The MNIST experiment is a proof of concept on 50 selected circuits with hardwired random sparse views, not a realistic scalable-oversight benchmark; the authors note that the verifier could estimate these majority outputs without a prover.; The general preprocessing step is not measured or amortized in the experiment. The implementation uses Ligero openings whose verifier cost grows with the square root of the trace rather than achieving the theorem’s polylogarithmic behavior.; The largest MNIST case leaves the prover about 60× slower than direct table-lookup evaluation. The GitHub README clarifies that experiment timings measure the honest prover’s messages and answers from retained data; they do not perform a machine-state restore, so end-to-end checkpoint/restore cost is unmeasured.; The repository provides code, result ledgers, scripts and selected input bundles, but a full rerun of the largest MNIST result is resource-intensive: the README specifies about 400 GB memory and a 1 TiB machine. Published bundles are author-provided; no rerun was performed here.; The BLAKE3 comparison uses modified interactive parameters and three runs on one core; it does not show end-to-end cost under matched deployment security assumptions.

Open evidence gaps: No independent proof review or pinned reproduction of the authors’ implementation was performed in this activation.; The experiments use selected hardwired circuits; reported timing runs do not restore a machine state, and the general preprocessing cost is not measured or amortized.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.40535v1 · https://github.com/ZiyiGuan/oversight-rip
8. Authors report unified likelihood-based training with accuracy, coverage and retention tradeoffs

Desk: training_data Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported data-mixture and continual-learning gains transfer across model scales and tasks, a shared likelihood objective could change how teams allocate training data and compute across pretraining and post-training. The score reflects that potential program-level consequence; experiments remain author-reported on 124M and 0.76B models with no independent reproduction or predictive scaling law.

What changed: A 67-page preprint frames pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning and suitable reinforcement-learning updates as likelihood fitting over a time-varying mixture of static data and successful model-generated targets. Its shared objective and trainer allow those sources to overlap; conventional staged training is a special case. The authors report controlled 124M-parameter reasoning-puzzle experiments and heterogeneous-data experiments with a 0.76B-parameter model. They report better accuracy, coverage, retention or continual-learning outcomes in several evaluated settings, alongside task and schedule tradeoffs. The paper explicitly describes the results as small-scale and does not establish predictive scaling laws or a universally preferred data mixture. Why it matters: If the reported results transfer across tasks and model scales, teams could treat data allocation across pretraining and post-training as one coupled design problem instead of selecting separate training algorithms for each stage. The evidence supports a potentially useful training framework and measured small-scale tradeoffs, not a general replacement recipe for frontier-model training.

Demonstrated: The arXiv record and full paper provide inspectable mathematical definitions, trainer description, experimental protocols and result tables. The paper publication and what its authors report are established; the numerical training outcomes have not been independently reproduced in this review.

Claimed: For a controlled 124M-parameter model trained on 20B pretraining tokens and a 510M-token reasoning-puzzle corpus, the authors report that selected unified mixtures improve accuracy or coverage against selected staged baselines at several compute budgets and retain more general benchmark performance than staged midtraining. In separate experiments with a 0.76B-parameter model and heterogeneous web, math, code and reasoning data, they report improved retention and better downstream coding RL for tested mixtures, with accuracy/coverage tradeoffs.

Mechanism: The paper represents each static or generated source with a prompt and target distribution, assigns time-varying mixture weights, and applies one maximum-likelihood loss to their mixture. Suitable reinforcement-learning objectives are recast as fitting success-conditioned model outputs; changing the data distribution and mixture schedule changes what is learned while the loss rule remains the same. Its practical trainer mixes static records and generated RL examples in a shared asynchronous data buffer.

Strongest baseline: Within the controlled experiment, staged training uses the same pretraining and midtraining sources, MaxRL objective, RL-update budgets and evaluation tasks; authors select the staged initialization by its final RL accuracy. Compute-frontier comparisons allow the best observed checkpoint under each total budget. In the heterogeneous experiment, staged and unified runs start from the described base model and use the same subsequent coding RL configuration; the paper includes an asynchronous-trainer 0% mixing ablation.

Regime: Author-run 124M-parameter controlled reasoning-puzzle experiments and 0.76B-parameter experiments with Math12K and a 240M-token heterogeneous midtraining corpus. Main controlled RL outcomes average two training seeds. Evaluation includes synthetic verifiable reasoning puzzles, math/coding benchmarks and held-out retention measures. The paper calls its evidence small-scale; most runs optimize one RL task at a time.

Limitations: All numerical outcomes in this record are author-reported; no independent reproduction or code artifact was inspected.; The controlled study uses a 124M-parameter model and synthetic verifiable reasoning puzzles; the separate heterogeneous-data study uses a 0.76B-parameter model. Neither establishes transfer to frontier-scale models.; The paper explicitly describes its empirical scope as small-scale, does not establish predictive scaling laws or a universally preferred mixture, and reports tradeoffs among accuracy, coverage and retention.; Most runs optimize a single RL task at a time. The results do not establish joint multi-task training behavior or advantages over long sequences of subsequent tasks.

Open evidence gaps: No independent implementation or reproduction of the paper's controlled or heterogeneous-data results was found in this review.; The paper's experiments cover 124M and 0.76B models and mainly one RL task at a time; scaling behavior and joint multi-task transfer remain unestablished.; The paper does not identify a generally optimal mixture or schedule, and does not establish a predictive method for selecting mixtures from model/task properties.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40564v1
9. ClinGeX reports improved clinical-genomics concordance with executable domain skills and clinician collaboration

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If replicated, improved expert concordance and reduced analysis time across clinical-genomics workflows could materially change how medical centres design and evaluate AI-assisted interpretation. The findings are limited to one author-reported preprint, three study scenarios and a small, self-selected non-interventional routine-use assessment; patient-outcome benefit and wider transfer are not established.

What changed: An arXiv paper introduces ClinGeX, a clinical-genomics agent organized around 105 executable skills selected and sequenced for each task. The authors report 71.7% macro-averaged task-level concordance across 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, compared with 45.7% for the strongest comparator. In a counterbalanced study across three centres, 45 clinical-genomics professionals completed 135 cases with ClinGeX, DeepSeek or no AI assistance; ClinGeX-assisted concordance was higher in all three scenarios. A separate one-month assessment collected 96 self-selected analysis-episode reports from 11 professionals, who reported frequent conclusion adoption and shorter analysis time. The real-use assessment was non-interventional and outputs could not affect patient care. All performance and workflow results remain author-reported; no independent reproduction or clinical-outcome trial was established. Why it matters: The study tests a domain-grounded agent across automated benchmarks, clinician collaboration and a bounded routine-work assessment, providing more decision-relevant evidence than a single synthetic task. If independently replicated, skill libraries that encode guidelines, evidence sources and analytical procedures could improve how clinical agents assemble auditable workflows. The results do not establish patient benefit or general performance beyond the evaluated settings.

Claimed: The authors report 71.7% macro-averaged task-level concordance over 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases versus 45.7% for the strongest comparator. In the counterbalanced clinician study, ClinGeX-assisted case concordance was 51.1% for criterion-level variant analysis, 57.8% for rare-disease interpretation and 64.4% for molecular oncology; human-only values were 22.2%, 28.9% and 31.1%, and DeepSeek-assisted values were 15.6%, 31.1% and 20.0%. Median time decreased from 60 to 15 minutes for variant analysis and 30 to 15 minutes for rare-disease interpretation; the oncology change from 15 to 11 minutes was not statistically significant. In the exploratory routine-use assessment, professionals reported fully or partially adopting conclusions in 91/96 episodes and saving at least five minutes in 90/96. These are author-reported metrics.

Mechanism: ClinGeX contains 105 curated executable skills—27 guidance, 40 search and 38 analysis skills—connected by semantic and prerequisite relationships. A task-specific selector retrieves relevant skills and prerequisites, then an LLM agent composes and executes an evidence-grounded analysis workflow.

Strongest baseline: The 223-case benchmark's strongest reported comparator scored 45.7% macro-averaged concordance. The human-AI study included both routine unaided work and DeepSeek assistance under a counterbalanced assignment. The routine-use assessment had no control condition.

Regime: Clinical-genomics interpretation tasks covering criterion-level variant analysis, rare-disease genomic interpretation and molecular-oncology decisions. The controlled reader study involved 45 professionals across three centres and 135 cases. The one-month routine-use assessment involved 11 experienced professionals and 96 self-selected analysis episodes.

Limitations: All benchmark, reader-study and workflow results are reported by the paper authors and have not been independently reproduced in this activation.; The reader study covered three scenarios and used expert-consensus concordance as a proxy for interpretive quality, not patient outcomes; several secondary comparisons were not statistically significant.; The prospective one-month assessment was non-interventional, self-selected and uncontrolled. ClinGeX outputs were not permitted to affect clinical reports, patient management or other clinical decisions.; The study does not establish generalization to other clinical-genomics areas, broader populations or care settings, nor independent clinical deployment efficacy.

Open evidence gaps: No independent team has reproduced the reported automated benchmark or clinician-collaboration results in this activation.; The authors state that ClinGeX source code is not publicly available; their bilingual deployed system requires registration, while study data are available upon reasonable request. The complete evaluated 105-skill package and exact configuration were not independently inspected.; Patient-care effects and clinical outcomes were not measured; the routine-use assessment was non-interventional and uncontrolled.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40556

items: Anthropic reports Claude leads 26% of measured AI R&D while none is fully autonomous — importance 8/10 · Anthropic published a prototype R&D Automation Index based on roughly 15,000 sampled granular R&D tasks organized into 378 leaf categories and rated on Epoch AI's AL0-AL5 automation scale. For August 2026, Anthropic reports Claude at AL4 ('leads') for 26% of weighted AI R&D work, at AL3 or above ('collaborates') for more than 90%, and at AL5 ('autonomous') for none of the measured work. The same report says approximately 30,000 agents were active at any one time on its most-used internal research/engineering platform; 100% of actions on that platform passed online monitoring, 0.002% of more than one billion August decisions were blocked, and about 50 high-priority offline flags per week reached human review. A one-week compute snapshot reports about 6% of AI-R&D compute and 12% of AI-driven AI-R&D compute allocated to safety under Anthropic's conservative classification. — FCMO-FDBE3D996243

A collaborative AI laboratory reports a theory-led diamond-spin experiment — importance 7/10 · A preprint reports a collaborative LLM-agent laboratory that derived and tested a calibration law for ensembles of nitrogen-vacancy spins in diamond. The agents rejected an initial design because ordinary interpolation could make the same predictions, then classified an acquisition as inconclusive when phase and reference controls failed during signal drift. Authors report that agents revised the protocol without relaxing precommitted criteria; a six-hour randomized acquisition then passed the stated controls and supported predictions on four withheld pulse sequences. These are author-reported results from one laboratory study. The public Auctopus repository’s README says its mock-model offline demo does not reproduce the paper and that study prompts are not included; experimental data and analysis are available from the corresponding author on request. — FCMO-F11300C510E8

OpenAI describes expanded frontier-model misalignment monitoring and a live training alert — importance 7/10 · OpenAI’s Oct 29 disclosure describes a layered system for monitoring frontier-model training, evaluations, internal agent use and selected external tool use. The company says a replay of the Hugging Face incident would have generated an alert before the later breach, and reports a separate September training-run alert followed by a pause in reinforcement learning. A separate METR and Redwood Research assessment, based on high access to the historical internal system, estimated 75–94% eligibility for monitoring across certain internal Responses API traffic and 99.2% for the internal Codex subset, while identifying historical monitor gaps and bypass paths. Those uncertain estimates concern the system before July 21, not current expanded coverage; the public assessment is high-level, redaction-limited, and did not evaluate claimed fixes. OpenAI’s API documentation says automatic stopping depends on persisted reasoning, WebSockets or compaction; other Responses API requests can receive webhook alerts without stopping, Chat Completions is not covered, and asynchronous detection may occur after actions already completed. — FCMO-87CD00EDD30A

items: Amazon reports 39% AWS growth and sharply higher Bedrock usage in Q3 — importance 5/10 · Amazon’s October 29, 2026 Q3 release reports AWS net sales of $46.0 billion, up 39% year over year, and AWS operating income of $17.8 billion. The company also reports Fortune 500 spending on Bedrock nearly 7x higher and Bedrock token volume nearly 17x higher year over year, while AgentCore was used by tens of thousands of customers who deployed twice as many agents in Q3 as in the prior three quarters combined. Amazon says its trailing-twelve-month free-cash-flow outflow was $42.4 billion, primarily reflecting a $94.8 billion year-over-year increase in net property and equipment purchases that primarily reflects AI investment. These are company-reported metrics. Amazon also expects approximately $220 billion in company-wide cash capital expenditures for 2026, without allocating that outlook to AI or AWS. The Q3 Form 10-Q adds cash capital expenditures of $75.9 billion in Q3 2026 versus $34.2 billion a year earlier, and $172.2 billion for the first nine months versus $89.9 billion; Amazon says most technology-infrastructure spending supports AWS growth and expects cash capex to rise meaningfully in 2027. These amounts remain company-wide or AWS-segment measures and are not allocated to AI services. The filing gives no AI-specific revenue, margin, utilization, token baseline or unit economics, so it does not establish that AI drove AWS growth or was profitable. — FCMO-7005EE35D313

items: FARMS links source-contextual Lean statements to bounded numerical skills — importance 5/10 · The authors report 157 accepted pipeline outcomes among 171 selected statements from four sources in randomized numerical linear algebra and numerical PDEs; three accepted cases carry source warnings. Two bounded applications use selected formal statements for heat-flow solving and wave-response compression. In a six-target comparison, their FARMS configuration cost less per target than a statement-level AutoformBot adaptation, but that adaptation allowed sorry in target and auxiliary proofs. No independent build or reproduction was performed, and the paper does not establish broad cross-domain transfer or autonomous discovery of new methods. — FCMO-8825A4D7BC22

OpenAI manuscript claims the irrationality exponent of π is exactly 2 — importance 8/10 · OpenAI’s 23-page manuscript claims that for every ν>2 there is a threshold Q(ν) such that |π−p/q|≥q^-ν for all integers p and q≥Q(ν), and concludes that π has irrationality exponent 2. If correct, this would sharply improve the prior upper bounds discussed in the paper. The threshold is ineffective; the manuscript does not prove a uniform c/q² lower bound or bounded continued-fraction partial quotients. OpenAI’s public family-017 note describes a Lean statement covering the exponent claim, but no independent build, semantic audit or number-theory review was performed here. Treat the theorem as claimed, not established. — FCMO-2FD75289C054

Rewindable proofs give weak verifiers a new route to check robust computations — importance 6/10 · A new paper introduces rewindable interactive proofs, in which a verifier can restore an AI prover to a saved interaction state and ask new questions from there. For robust oracle computations, the authors prove a relativizing protocol with a succinct verifier and a linear-time honest prover, without assuming that a prover is truthful or using cryptography. The paper reports a proof-of-concept MNIST experiment and a BLAKE3 comparison, while explicitly saying the experiments are not a realistic scalable-oversight benchmark. A linked public repository supplies code, result ledgers and scripts, but clarifies that timed runs do not restore a machine state; general preprocessing and real model-state restoration costs remain unresolved, so deployed oversight benefits are not established. — FCMO-2887BE11D4BC

Fengyun satellite extreme-weather AI model announced at official conference; media report names two systems — importance 5/10 · The Hunan Provincial Government reports that a Fengyun satellite extreme-weather AI model was formally released at the National Satellite Meteorological Center-hosted user conference on 29 October 2026. A Chinese-language Science and Technology Daily article hosted by Beijing’s NCSTI names two systems: a typhoon image-interpretation model and a short-range severe-convection warning model. It reports their intended functions and timing specifications, but no forecast-skill evaluation or deployment evidence was inspected. The government event report confirms a model release; the two variant identities and performance figures remain attributed reporting. — FCMO-1EDFA7543E05

items: OpenAI offers GPT-6 Astra’s weights as GPT-Rosalind-6 for screened life-sciences research — importance 5/10 · OpenAI’s Oct 30 system-card addendum says GPT-Rosalind-6 uses GPT-6 Astra’s weights without additional training or post-training. OpenAI’s release and setup notes say GPT-6 Rosalind Research is rolling out to limited approved Research organizations in Work and Codex, and through separately approved API access; it is not available in Chat. Enterprise workspaces begin with a two-week Admin Preview with access off by default. At the highest reasoning budget tested, OpenAI reports higher GPT-Rosalind-6 scores than GPT-Rosalind-5.5 on three shared benchmark sets: MedChemBench v7 (49.6% vs 28.9%, 99 problems), GeneBench Pro v13 single-attempt success (37.7% vs 16.7%, 129 problems), and LifeSciBench Gold (61.3% vs 44.0%, 94 of 100 problems after excluding six flagged tasks). OpenAI classifies biological capability as High but below Critical on its selected Preparedness evaluations. These are first-party results; GeneBench used a configuration unlike production, the Critical thresholds are preliminary, and no independent reproduction or real-world productivity/safety outcome is established. — FCMO-430A20BC3FD2

blocks.text: policy_geopolitics

items: Japan begins phased government AI-agent rollout under a new governance standard — importance 6/10 · Japan’s Digital Agency announced a staged expansion of Government AI Gennai to agent workflows and published a governance, security and safety standard. On October 30, it said a prototype app for parliamentary-answer drafting would be offered to about 180,000 government employees for trial use; 102 staff from 16 ministries had helped evaluate its development. The agency reports about 80% of evaluator-survey respondents wanted to use the prototype, without stating the respondent count or survey method. Human review and final responsibility remain with staff. This establishes reported intent, not adoption or measured performance. — FCMO-8BF3C32CA3BF

India’s telecom regulator opens consultation on responsible AI-use guidelines — importance 5/10 · On 30 October 2026, India’s Telecom Regulatory Authority (TRAI) opened a consultation on draft AI guidance for authorised entities using AI in telecom networks or services; comments are due 27 November. The 12-page proposal would require board-approved internal policies, system risk classification and inventory, pre-deployment assessments, incident and user-harm recording, senior governance oversight, and reporting of high- and critical-severity incidents. It is a consultation draft, not a final rule. Adoption, provider implementation, costs and operational effects remain unestablished. — FCMO-D2CC53FB8BD7

Japan Digital Agency survey reports self-reported time savings and uneven uptake for government AI Gennai — importance 5/10 · Japan’s Digital Agency published the first usage survey for Gennai, its government generative-AI environment. The questionnaire received 6,439 responses from government employees across ministries and related bodies; the satisfaction and task-time results reported here use a 3,078-person subset. The Agency reports 71.7% satisfaction in that subset and estimates about 1.83 hours saved per user per week from self-reported task-time bands. Its materials differ slightly on the share reporting at least one hour saved: 54.4% on the release page and detailed PDF page, versus 54.5% on the PDF overview slide. The estimate uses band midpoints, caps “10+ hours saved” at 10, and treats unknown/no-change responses as zero. About 31.2% of all 6,439 respondents said they rarely or never used Gennai. These are first-party survey responses and an assumption-based estimate, not independently measured time savings or causal evidence. — FCMO-339365DC7ACA

UK regulators state existing rules apply to personal AI agents — importance 4/10 · On 30 October 2026, the UK Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum’s four member regulators—the CMA, FCA, ICO and Ofcom—issued a joint statement on personal AI agents. They said existing competition, consumer, data-protection, online-safety, financial-services, payments and cybersecurity frameworks apply, and described ongoing coordination, engagement with firms, guidance, intelligence sharing and regulatory sandboxes. The statement does not create a new legal duty or provide final agent-specific rules, a named enforcement action or measured implementation results. — FCMO-67F54C0B04E1
